findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

additional_observations: No mass, midline shift or hydrocephalus
ct.impression: Non-contrast CT head: no acute intracranial abnormality. Impression: normal non-contrast CT of the head.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

findings.description: 3 Hz trains of 10 stimuli; skin temperature 33 C; no anticholinesterase medication taken.
Baseline CMAP 2.1 mV; decrement 1st to 4th response 7%.
Baseline CMAP 9.6 mV; decrement 2%. After 10 s maximal contraction CMAP 9.9 mV (3% increment); no post-exercise facilitation.

output.impression: 1. No decrement greater than 10% at 3 Hz in nasalis, trapezius or abductor digiti minimi. 2. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes; no post-exercise facilitation. Normal repetitive nerve stimulation study. Single-fiber EMG recommended if a disorder of neuromuscular transmission remains suspected.

findings.description: 20 fiber pairs analysed. Mean consecutive difference (MCD) 54 microseconds (reference <35). Increased jitter in 11 of 20 pairs (55%); impulse blocking in 16% of pairs.
findings.muscle: Left orbicularis oculi (voluntary activation, concentric needle)

output.impression: Abnormal single-fiber EMG of the left orbicularis oculi: increased jitter (mean MCD 54 microseconds) with impulse blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Increased jitter is not specific; clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description: MRD1 1.0 mm before; ice pack over the closed left lid for 2 minutes; MRD1 3.5 mm immediately after (improvement 2.5 mm).
MRD1 4.0 mm, no ptosis; not tested.

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: left MRD1 improved by 2.5 mm after 2 minutes of cooling (positive threshold 2 mm).

output.interpretation: Anti-GQ1b IgG not detected (<1:100). Anti-GQ1b antibodies are found in most patients with Miller Fisher syndrome; a negative result does not exclude it. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: FVC 3.02 L (92% predicted, 39 mL/kg), MIP -68 cmH2O and MEP 88 cmH2O within reference limits. Normal respiratory muscle function.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 7.6 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; TSH and free T4 normal
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable asymmetric ptosis and ophthalmoparesis with a Cogan lid twitch: AChR binding antibody is the first-line serological test (positive in about half of ocular MG), and TSH screens for coexisting autoimmune thyroid disease, which also enters the differential of eyelid swelling with restricted eye movements (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli A et al., Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: SFEMG of left orbicularis oculi: mean MCD 54 microseconds with blocking in 16% of pairs; RNS of nasalis, trapezius and ADM without significant decrement
action_criteria.label: Confirm the neuromuscular transmission defect electrophysiologically (single-fiber EMG of a facial muscle or repetitive nerve stimulation)
action_criteria.rationale: Repetitive nerve stimulation is normal in more than half of patients with ocular MG; single-fiber EMG of a facial muscle is the more sensitive study, although increased jitter is not specific. Either study satisfies the electrodiagnostic step (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left MRD1 improved from 1.0 mm to 3.5 mm after 2 minutes of ice
action_criteria.label: Perform the ice pack test on the ptotic left eyelid
action_criteria.rationale: Left ptosis on examination: an improvement of MRD1 by at least 2 mm after 2-5 minutes of cooling supports a disorder of neuromuscular transmission at the bedside, at no cost.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; thymic involution appropriate for age
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast to look for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG, including ocular MG, because a thymoma would change management (thoracic surgery) (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.label: Test anti-GQ1b IgG if Miller Fisher syndrome is still considered
action_criteria.rationale: Ophthalmoparesis raises Miller Fisher syndrome, but there is no ataxia, areflexia or antecedent infection; anti-GQ1b is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 92% predicted (39 mL/kg), MIP -68 cmH2O and MEP 88 cmH2O, all normal
action_criteria.label: Measure baseline respiratory function
action_criteria.rationale: Purely ocular disease without bulbar or limb weakness: a baseline FVC, MIP and MEP is optional and serves as a reference if the disease generalizes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General guidance on ocular MG treatment
action_criteria.label: Review guidance on the treatment of ocular myasthenia gravis
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading on treatment and prognosis; not a clinical step in the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis and diplopia to a brainstem vascular cause (or start secondary stroke prevention for presumed TIA) before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
required_recommendations: Diagnose AChR antibody-positive ocular myasthenia gravis (MGFA class I): fatigable asymmetric left ptosis with a Cogan lid twitch and variable ophthalmoparesis with an INO-like pattern, AChR binding antibody 7.6 nmol/L, increased jitter with blocking on single-fiber EMG, positive ice pack test, normal brain and orbit imaging, no thymoma on mediastinal CT.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three times daily, titrating to effect up to 60 mg four to five times daily, with advice on muscarinic side effects.

If ptosis or diplopia remain disabling on pyridostigmine, add low-dose prednisone (10-20 mg/day, increasing by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days to the lowest effective dose) with bone protection, and monitor blood pressure, glucose and potassium (she takes hydrochlorothiazide) [Sanders_2016].

Counsel that about half of patients with ocular MG generalize, mostly within 2 years, and to seek care at once for swallowing, speech, limb or breathing weakness; arrange neurology follow-up at regular intervals over the first 2 years.
Give the patient a written list of medicines that can worsen MG (fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, IV magnesium, beta-blockers including timolol eye drops) to show every prescriber.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a disorder of the neuromuscular junction (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
CSF has no role in MG; Miller Fisher syndrome, the only CSF-related mimic here, is unlikely without ataxia or areflexia and is tested by serum anti-GQ1b (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; mediastinal CT covers thymoma screening (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to the diagnosis of ocular MG.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis of ocular MG.

accepted: Ocular myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive (MGFA Class I)

differential.diagnosis: Brainstem lesion with internuclear ophthalmoplegia (stroke, TIA or demyelination)
differential.key_features: INO-like pattern raised it, but MRI brain with MRA shows no brainstem or MLF lesion, there is no abducting nystagmus, and the ptosis is fatigable with a Cogan lid twitch.

Eyelid swelling and restricted elevation could suggest it, but there is no proptosis or lid retraction, the orbits are normal on imaging, TSH and free T4 are normal and the deficit is fatigable rather than restrictive.
Hypertension is a risk factor, but the deficit involves both eyes, fits no single nerve, fluctuates and is accompanied by fatigable ptosis.
Eyelid swelling, but no fever, pain on eye movement, chemosis or proptosis, and normal orbits on imaging.
Ophthalmoparesis, but no ataxia, areflexia or antecedent infection; anti-GQ1b negative if tested.
Two-week fluctuating course, fatigability, Cogan lid twitch and positive AChR antibodies are against a slowly progressive mitochondrial myopathy.

key_clinical_evidence: Fatigable asymmetric left ptosis with a Cogan lid twitch and variable ophthalmoparesis with an INO-like pattern, pupils spared, limbs and bulbar function normal.
AChR binding antibody 7.6 nmol/L with elevated blocking antibody; MuSK negative; TSH and free T4 normal.
Single-fiber EMG of the left orbicularis oculi: mean MCD 54 microseconds with blocking in 16% of pairs; RNS of nasalis, trapezius and ADM without significant decrement, as is common in ocular MG.
Ice pack test: left MRD1 improved from 1.0 to 3.5 mm.
Brain MRI with MRA and MRV and orbital CT before referral were normal; no brainstem lesion explains the eye movements.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma; here it shows age-appropriate thymic involution.
About half of patients with ocular MG generalize, mostly within 2 years; follow-up and patient education are part of management.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An INO needs an MLF lesion; the normal brain MRI, the absent abducting nystagmus and the fatigable ptosis with Cogan lid twitch point to a pseudo-INO of neuromuscular junction origin.
red_herrings.data_point: INO-like pattern suggesting a brainstem lesion or TIA
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pseudo-INO with bilateral horizontal restriction mimics true INO from brainstem lesion

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: No fever, chemosis, proptosis or pain on eye movement, and normal orbital imaging: orbital infection or inflammation is excluded.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Eyelid swelling + restricted eye movement can resemble orbital cellulitis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal MRI and MRA exclude a vascular cause; the fluctuating, fatigable bilateral pattern is not microvascular.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Hypertension raises pre-test probability for TIA/stroke as cause of focal neurological signs

ocular myasthenia gravis.query: ocular myasthenia gravis diagnosis and treatment

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In ocular MG, corticosteroids are advised when the response to pyridostigmine is unsatisfactory.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: Disease that remains purely ocular is called ocular myasthenia; a large proportion of patients presenting with ocular symptoms develop generalized weakness, most within the first two years.
results.source: Gilhus NE, N Engl J Med 2016;375:2570-2581

ocular myasthenia gravis.summary: Consensus guidance: AChR antibody testing first, MuSK when AChR is negative, RNS or single-fiber EMG for electrodiagnostic confirmation, thymic imaging in all patients; corticosteroids for ocular MG not controlled by pyridostigmine. Generalization occurs in many patients presenting with ocular symptoms, mostly within two years.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 52-year-old African American woman with hypertension was admitted with a 2-week history of bilateral eyelid swelling, double vision, and abnormal eye movements. She reported blurred vision that fluctuated in severity, with the right eye appearing more affected. She initially noticed left upper eyelid swelling and heaviness, followed by diplopia on rightward gaze. She denied fever, photophobia, jaw or swallowing difficulty, limb weakness, numbness, or gait disturbance. She had no preceding infections, vaccinations, or recent travel.

On examination, swelling of the left upper eyelid was prominent. Extraocular movement testing revealed the right eye failed to move fully in the horizontal plane, and the left eye had impaired adduction with preserved abduction, producing an internuclear ophthalmoplegia-like pattern. The left upper eyelid was ptotic. On upgaze, the left eye failed to fully elevate. A Cogan lid twitch sign was elicited in the left eye on downgaze and return to primary position. Visual acuity and fundoscopy were normal. The rest of the neurological examination was unremarkable.

Given the internuclear ophthalmoplegia-like pattern, the admitting team first considered a brainstem structural lesion or TIA and obtained urgent imaging on the day of admission: CT of the orbits, MRI of the brain, MRA and MRV were all reported as unremarkable. She was then referred to neurology for further evaluation of the eye movement disorder.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Left upper eyelid ptosis with periorbital swelling. Cogan lid twitch positive (left). Right eye: limited horizontal movement in both directions. Left eye: impaired adduction with preserved abduction, without abducting nystagmus. Left eye: failure to fully elevate on upgaze. No nystagmus. Visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally. Pupils equal and reactive. No proptosis. No pain on eye movement.
neurological_exam.motor: Motor exam 5/5 all limbs. No fasciculations.
